author: Platform Documentation
deck: A practical tour of the record, contract, lifecycle, and multisite boundaries that make agent publishing predictable.
description: Understand why pages, sections, navigation, taxonomy, site settings, templates, themes, products, articles, tracking, and editorial voice share one governed lifecycle.

public.body: A page route, a footer menu, a theme palette, and an article look unrelated in the browser. In the CMS they are all typed records. Each record has an id, a site owner, a schema-bound body, publication state, review state, a lock, version counters, and history. That common envelope lets one toolchain manage every surface without inventing a separate workflow for each feature.
public.title: One model, many surfaces

public.body: Before changing an object, an agent reads its object contract. The contract declares required fields, exact patch operations, validation rules, creation policy, approval policy, media limits, and recovery steps. This makes the running platform the source of truth; prose documentation explains the model, while the contract decides what is currently legal.
public.title: The contract is the live API

public.body: An edit begins with checkout. Typed patch operations run under that lease and carry the expected record version, so concurrent drift fails loudly. Validation checks schema, references, reader safety, renderability, and publish readiness. Operations preserve an inverse, which makes deliberate rollback possible without bypassing governance.
public.title: Writes are leased and reversible

public.body: Publishing validates the draft, materializes a derived export, commits it with a deployment skip marker, and stamps the published revision. It does not spend a production build. A separate release batches all accumulated exports into one deploy and confirms that the production site is serving the target commit.
public.title: Publish is not release

public.body: Every tenant has its own site directory, object store, policies, credentials, and deployment, while the renderer and publishing engine live in shared core packages. A core fix can propagate across the fleet through CI; a client content change remains isolated to that tenant. The result is reuse at the software layer and separation at the data and authority layers.
public.title: Multisite without content forks
